catalog_quote: 2. Tone. Maꞌdi Urúléti is spoken with tone. There are three main tone levels: high, mid, and low. The tone marks are placed above the vowels. High tone is marked with a line slanting up, low tone is marked with a line slanting down, while mid tone is unmarked. ... A few examples of why using tone marks is important for writing: orí 'snake', òrì 'fear', òrí 'lice'; tí 'cow', ti 'mouth', tì 'to flood'. ... 3. Long vowels ... Long vowels are written with the same letter twice. Each vowel is marked for tone.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Southern Ma'di (Ma'di Urúléti, Okollo) is a tone language with three level tones (high, mid, low), lexically contrastive (minimal triplets on monosyllables and disyllables); every vowel, including each half of a long vowel, bears its own tone. Nothing is said about word stress/accent.
new_statements.exceptions: none; contour tones not discussed in this leaflet (the unpublished Stolen 2020 phonology ms. has a 'Contour tones' section)
new_statements.identity_note: Ma'di Urúléti = 'Upper Ma'di' = Ma'di Okollo / Ma'di South, Madi-Okollo District, Uganda; SIL archives file it under Subject Language 'Southern Ma'di [snm]' and record 93283 calls Ma'di Uruleti 'a variety of the Southern Ma'di language [snm] spoken in Uganda'; contact address Okollo Community Centre. Not Moyo/Lokai Ma'di [mhi] and not standard Lugbara [lgg].

new_statements.quote: However, the linguists soon realized that they were actually sorting by the tones and not by vowel quality. In other words, the functional load of tone was so high that the participants were not able to pay attention to other phonological distinctions. This led to a modification in the workshop plan: it was clear that tone markings would need to be determined first. Together we practiced identifying high, mid and low tones, and went through each pile of cards together adding the correct tone marks,[fn. 3] ... [fn. 3:] These surface tones appeared to be stable throughout the grammar, with minimal or no interaction with other tones. Representing three tone levels in the orthography is sufficient for reading, but there seems to be at least one additional surface or underlying tone level.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ma'di Urule is a tone language with three contrastive tone levels (high, mid, low) carrying a very high functional load; the linguist notes at least one further surface or underlying tone level beyond the three. surface tones stable across the grammar with little or no tonal interaction; all syllables V or CV, no codas or clusters. Nothing is said about word stress or accent anywhere in the chapter (the words 'stress'/'accent' do not occur).
new_statements.exceptions: fn. 3: 'at least one additional surface or underlying tone level' beyond H/M/L; sec. 3.3 lists 'Do the tones interact with adjacent tones? Are there grammatical tones?' as workshop research questions without reporting answers; sec. 3.1: no phonemic ATR contrast in mid vowels (7-vowel orthography), slight ATR difference in /o/ heard by linguists only.
new_statements.identity_note: Exactly this languoid: 'The Maꞌdi Urule community lives in the West Nile Region of Northwestern Uganda and call their language Maꞌdi Uruleti. The most similar language is Lugbara [lgg]. Other languages in the Moru-Maꞌdi language family in Uganda include Aringa [luc] and Maꞌdi North/Moyo/Adjumani [mhi]' (p. 167); population 60,000 in Maꞌdi Okollo District; fn. 1 'Urule "upper" refers to the location as being further up the Nile'. Author is the SIL Uganda linguist who ran the March 2020 orthography workshop (12 days, 9 Ma'di Urule speakers + 2 linguists, 1700-item SILCAWL) and wrote the unpublished 2021 phonology ms. (SIL archives 93283, PASS-1 pointer). First-hand, peer-edited case study; not a phonology paper (contents 'other' = orthography-development case study with phonological findings). | Names the language 'Ma'di Okollo' throughout and places it in 'the Moru-Ma'di subfamily' of Nilo-Saharan, contrasting it with Aringa (4 tones); hosted under the ISO path /snm/ of the Ma'di Okollo site that SIL Uganda's own menu labels 'Ma'di Okollo (Southern)' -> Southern Ma'di [snm] = sout2828 exactly (Okollo = Glottolog dialect name; not Moyo/Lokai Ma'di [mhi], not standard Lugbara [lgg]). Documents the EARLIER (2011 trial / 2014) Ma'di Okollo orthography -- dieresis for a mid-high tone, circumflex for rising, under-dots for heavy [+ATR] vowels -- which the 2020 Stølen workshop replaced (ɨ ʉ letters, three marked tone levels); follows the SIL Sudan-branch 'why mark tone' template. First-hand (SIL fieldworker + committee), unrefereed literacy advocacy material, hence texts-or-primer.

new_statements.quote: The Maꞌdi Okollo language is also a tonal language (with 5 tones plus falling and rising combinations). For example, ‘oori’ can be many different words with different meanings depending on the tone, but you can't tell which meaning it has just by looking at it ... In fact, the Moru-Maꞌdi subfamily is highly tonal. ... [p. 3 'Tone':] The Maꞌdi Okollo language has 5 tones: High (á), Mid-high (ä), Flat (a), Low (à), Rising (â). ... Any vowel that is unmarked has a Flat tone. Combinations of falling (áà) and rising (àá) tones can occur. These combinations are written with tones on two vowels ... [p. 6:] The tone plays an important role in the verb system of the Maꞌdi Okollo language. The tone of a verb changes in different grammatical situations. For example, ori means “it settles” while orí means “they settle”. All the tones can be found in the verb system

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ma'di Okollo is described as a tone language with five distinctive tones in the 2014 orthography -- High, Mid-high, 'Flat' (unmarked), Low and Rising -- plus falling/rising two-vowel combinations (áà, áä, àa, àá); tone distinguishes lexical items (rụ́ 'name' / rụ̈ 'sudden' / rụ 'seize' / rụ̀ 'sound of falling' / rụ̂ 'suddenly'; ori 'god' / òri 'seed' / orí 'they settle') and carries grammatical load in the verb (ti jó 'he thatches' vs tí jó 'they thatch', negation paradigms by tone); vowels contrast Light vs Heavy (tongue-root/ATR, heavy under-dotted; /a/ always light). Nothing is said about stress, accent or syllable prominence (the words do not occur).
new_statements.exceptions: None on stress. On tone: the 2014 five-way list (four levels + Rising) differs from the later SIL analysis (2022 leaflet, Stølen 2024) that writes three levels H/M/L and notes 'at least one additional surface or underlying tone level' -- the number of contrastive levels (3 vs 4) is unsettled between the 2014 and 2020 orthographies.

sources.note: Group-level survey statement: 'Even such intimately closely allied languages as MORU and MA'DI have quite different stress behaviour. In MORU stress is on the first syllable of disyllabic words.. In MA'DI, however, stress is on the final vowel: ˈléndrị, ˈléndr, iˈza, lɛ̀ˈdra. In both languages words within a phrase retain their original stress.' Nothing said about LUGBARA stress or about Okollo varieties. (Their MA'DI = Moyo/Sudan Ma'di [mhi].)

sources.note: Lugbara (Aivu/Arua dialect). Phonology + ch. 2 'Intonation' treat tone only (three level tones plus glides, verb tone rules); no statement on word stress ('Stressing of verbs' secs. 426-30 in the contents is grammatical emphasis). Intro sec. 7 p. viii: 'The most distant dialect is apparently that of the Ma'di-Ndri (also called Màdé) of the Olepi-Okolo area' -- i.e. Crazzolara counts the Okollo speech as a Logbara dialect but gives Ma'di-Ndri forms only exceptionally.

sources.note: Community orthography guide whose first content chapters are 'Tone -- Tone in Plural -- Nouns -- Tone in Verbs -- Tone Sequences' before vowels and consonants, i.e. it teaches the tone-marking conventions of the Urúléti orthography (which, per the works listed here, marks H/M/L on every vowel) including grammatical tone in plurals and verbs.
